passages.title: Glorification, then the exile of Banu an-Nadir
passages.tafsir:
This passage opens with the whole universe glorifying Allah, then shows that glorification worked out in history: the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banu an-Nadir from Madinah after they broke their treaty and plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ. Ayah 1 names Allah as **al-ʿAzīz** (the Almighty) and **al-Ḥakīm** (the All-Wise); ayat 2–5 are those two names in action — overwhelming power that emptied fortresses the Muslims never expected to control, and wisdom that measured the outcome rather than annihilating.

## The surah that carries a tribe's name

Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn ʿAbbas used to call this chapter "Surah Bani an-Nadir." Saʿid bin Mansur recorded that Saʿid bin Jubayr said: "I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about Surat al-Hashr and he said, 'It was revealed about Bani an-Nadir.'" Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it through another chain from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Ishaq said that the whole of Surat al-Hashr was revealed about them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the link backwards: the preceding surah condemned the close friendship the hypocrites had built with the Jews of Madinah; this one describes the punishment that came upon them, exile in this world and grievous torment in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 1: the tasbīḥ that frames it all

Ibn Kathir explains that everything in the heavens and on the earth praises Allah, glorifies Him, reveres Him, prays to Him and affirms His Oneness. He brings the parallel verse: *"The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein glorify Him, and there is not a thing but glorifies His praise. But you understand not their glorification"* (17:44). Creation is not silent; we are not tuned to hear it.

**Al-ʿAzīz**, Ibn Kathir says, means "of invincible majesty." **Al-Ḥakīm** means All-Wise "in what He decrees and legislates." ʿAzīz explains how a siege of six days undid forts that, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the Muslims did not think they would ever control. Ḥakīm explains why the outcome was exile with camel-loads of possessions rather than slaughter — and why, in ayah 5, even the Companions' disagreement over cutting date palms lands inside Allah's permission.

## What actually happened

**The treaty.** When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah he made a peace treaty with the Jews: he would not fight them and they would not fight him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records further clauses — they would not aid those taking up arms against the Muslims, and if the Jews were attacked the Muslims would assist them — with the details available in the *Sīrah* of Ibn Hisham. Banu an-Nadir were one of three signatory tribes, settled with their fortresses and orchards a couple of miles outside Madinah.

**Why this tribe, of all tribes.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a detail that makes the betrayal ache. Banu an-Nadir were descendants of the Prophet Harun (peace be upon him). Their forefathers were scholars of the Torah, which contained a full description of the Last Prophet ﷺ — his physical features, his signs of prophethood, his migration to Yathrib. They had *migrated from Syria and settled in Yathrib on purpose*, under the impression that he would be from Harun's line and that they would have the pleasure of his company. Some of their contemporaries saw his features and signs and recognised him as the Final Messenger — but because he was raised among the descendants of Ismaʿil (peace be upon him) they were disappointed, and jealousy stopped what recognition had already begun. Their certainty rose when they saw the victory at Badr, and was shaken when the Muslims suffered a temporary setback at Uhud — which, as Maʿārif notes, is a weak yardstick: distinguishing truth from falsehood by the measure of apparent victory and defeat. Ibn Kathir puts the same point in ayah 4's language: they denied the good news Allah had sent in the Books of earlier Messengers about the coming of Muhammad ﷺ, though "the Jews knew these facts about Muhammad ﷺ just as they knew their own children."

**The build-up.** After Uhud, Kaʿb ibn Ashraf, a leader of Banu an-Nadir, travelled to Makkah with a caravan of forty men. He and Abu Sufyan with forty of the pagan Quraysh entered the Sacred Mosque, held on to the covering of the House of Allah, and pledged that they would jointly fight the Muslims and annihilate them. When Kaʿb returned to Madinah, Jibra'il (peace be upon him) descended and informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the entire episode; the command was issued, and the Companion Muhammad ibn Maslamah carried it out.

**Bi'r Maʿunah and the blood money.** About seventy Companions sent to teach the Qur'an and preach Islam were killed at Bi'r Maʿunah — a request for teachers later discovered to be a mere conspiracy. Only ʿAmr ibn Umayyah ad-Damri escaped. On the road home he came upon two men and killed them — not knowing they were of Bani ʿAmir and held a promise of safe passage from the Prophet ﷺ. When he reported it, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"You have killed two men, I shall pay the blood money for them."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here: the agreements of the Muslims were not like the political agreements of today, in which every effort is made to find ways to escape or violate them. For the Prophet ﷺ and the early sincere Muslims, whatever the tongue uttered or the pen wrote was treated as part of religion and divine law, and binding. So the Prophet ﷺ first collected the blood-wit from the Muslims, and then — because Banu an-Nadir and Bani ʿAmir were allies bound by treaty — went to Banu an-Nadir to ask their help with it.

**The wall.** Ibn Ishaq's account: they said, "Yes, O Abu al-Qasim! We will help you, since you asked us for help." Then, meeting each other in secret while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat next to the wall of one of their houses, they said: "You will not find a better chance with this man than this." Who will ascend this wall and drop a stone on him? ʿAmr bin Jihash bin Kaʿb volunteered and went up. The Prophet ﷺ was sitting with several of his Companions, among them Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli. The news of the plot was conveyed to him from heaven; he stood up and went back to Madinah. The Companions went to look for him, learned that he had entered the city, followed him, and heard the news of the plot.

**The siege.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the tribe was sent word that they had ten days in which to leave. ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy stopped them, saying he had an army of two thousand men willing to lay down their lives to protect them; Ruh ul-Maʿani, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, names Wadiʿah ibn Malik, Suwaid and Ra'ish alongside him. Banu an-Nadir sent word that they would not leave. So the Prophet ﷺ marched with the Companions, and they locked themselves into their fortresses — and the hypocrites, being cowards, hid themselves. The Jews waited for support that never came; Allah cast terror into their hearts, and they asked for safe passage.

**The terms.** They could take whatever their camels could carry, except weapons. They took so much that a man would demolish his own house around its door so the door could go on his camel's back — Maʿārif lists hooks, latches, doors, planks, beams and rafters. Bani an-Nadir moved to Khaybar, and some went to Ash-Sham; Ibn Kathir mentions Adhriʿat. What remained was left to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who had control over how it was to be divided, and Allah says of it in the next ayah that for it "you made no expedition with either cavalry or camelry" (59:6). He divided it among the emigrants, giving none of the Ansar a share except two who said they were poor, Sahl bin Hunayf and Abu Dujanah Simak bin Kharashah. Only two men of Banu an-Nadir embraced Islam and thereby saved their wealth; Ibn Ishaq names them as Yamin bin ʿUmayr and Abu Saʿd bin Wahb. Ibn Ishaq reports that the campaign occurred after Uhud and Bi'r Maʿunah; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places it in Rabiʿ al-Awwal, 4 AH.

## Reading the words of ayat 2–3

**"At the first gathering" (li-awwal al-ḥashr).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ḥashr* means gathering or mustering — the word after which the surah is named — and gives two readings. Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani: it may refer to the *Muslims'* gathering, meaning Banu an-Nadir were made to leave the city at the first mustering of the Muslims, without fighting; or to the *Jews'* gathering for emigration, meaning this was their first exile, with a subtle indication that a second would follow. Maulana Thanawi gives the same two reasons, adding that the later evacuation of the Arabian Peninsula happened in the caliphate of ʿUmar, when he banished the Jews settled at Khaybar and ordered all the Jews to leave the peninsula. So Banu an-Nadir's is the "first banishment," ʿUmar's the "second."

**"You did not think that they would get out."** Ibn Kathir explains: you did not think it would happen within the few days you laid siege against them. The Companions had surrounded their forts for only six days, and those forts were fortified and formidable.

**"And they thought their fortresses would defend them from Allah! But Allah reached them from a place they expected not."** Ibn Kathir: there came to them from Allah what they did not expect or anticipate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān clarifies that the phrase "Allah came to them" means the command of Allah and His obedient angels came. Ibn Kathir sets beside it: *"Those before them indeed plotted, but Allah struck at the foundation of their building, and then the roof fell down upon them from above them, and the torment overtook them from directions they did not perceive"* (16:26). The defences were real. They were simply pointed the wrong way.

**"And He cast terror into their hearts."** Ibn Kathir: Allah cast fear, terror and fright in their hearts — and why would that not happen to them? The one who laid siege to them was he who was given victory by Allah frightening his enemies the distance of a month's journey. May Allah's peace and blessings be upon the Prophet.

**"They demolished their own dwellings with their own hands and the hands of the believers."** Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Ishaq and ʿUrwah bin az-Zubayr and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, explains that they brought down from their roofs and doors what they wanted to transport, so as to carry it on camels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the second half: while the Jews locked themselves up in their fortresses, the Muslims destroyed the trees and homes outside the fortresses to make them surrender. Between greed and siege, nothing was left standing — and the ayah lets you watch a man tear down his own house with his own hands.

**"Then take admonition, O you with eyes" (fa-ʿtabirū yā ulī l-abṣār).** Ibn Kathir: "Contemplate the end of those who defied Allah's command, contradicted His Messenger and denied His Book. See how Allah's humiliating torment struck them in this life, as well as the painful torment that Allah has reserved for them in the Hereafter." Eyes that only see camels and doorframes have not obeyed the command.

**Ayah 3: "Had Allah not decreed exile for them…"** Here the early authorities differ. Az-Zuhri held that were it not that Allah had already decreed that they would evacuate Madinah, leaving their homes and wealth behind, He would have sent another type of punishment upon them — being killed and captured. ʿUrwah, as-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said that Allah decreed that they would be punished in the life of this world and face the torment of the Fire in the Hereafter. Either way, the closing clause is fixed: Ibn Kathir says of "theirs shall be the torment of the Fire" that it is a matter ordained which they will surely face.

**Ayah 4: "That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger."** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah prepared this specific punishment and sent His Messenger ﷺ and his Companions against them because they defied Allah and His Messenger and denied the good news sent forth in the Books of previous Messengers regarding the coming of Muhammad ﷺ. Then: *"whosoever opposes Allah, then verily, Allah is Severe in punishment."* The tribe is the case study; the principle is general.

## Ayah 5: the date palms, and the Companions' question

**What is a *līnah*?** Ibn Kathir reports that līnah is an especially good type of date tree. Abu ʿUbaydah said it is a different kind of date from ʿAjwah and Barni; several others said it refers to every type of date except ʿAjwah; Ibn Jarir said it refers to all kinds of date trees, and quoted Mujahid that it also includes the Buwayrah type.

**Why they were cut.** Ibn Kathir: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laid siege to Banu an-Nadir, in order to humiliate them and bring fear and terror to their hearts, he ordered their date trees to be cut down. The Jews called out to him — "O Muhammad! You used to forbid mischief in the earth and blame those who did it. Why is it that you had the date trees cut down and burned?" Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated from Yazid bin Ruman, Qatadah and Muqatil bin Hayyan that Allah sent down this honourable ayah in answer: whatever līnah was felled or left intact by the Muslims was done by His permission, will, leave and pleasure, to humiliate and disgrace the enemy.

**The Companions' own unease.** Mujahid said that some of the emigrants discouraged others from chopping down the date trees, saying that they were war spoils for the Muslims; the Qur'an approved the actions of those who discouraged and of those who approved of cutting, stating that both did so only by Allah's leave. An-Nasa'i recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas that when the Muslims were ordered to cut the trees they hesitated, and some of them said: "We cut down some and left some. We must ask Allah's Messenger ﷺ if we will earn a reward for what we cut and if we will be burdened for what we left intact." Then this ayah was revealed.

The Two Sahihs record from Ibn ʿUmar that he ﷺ burned down the date trees of Banu an-Nadir and had the date palms of al-Buwayrah cut down, and that Allah revealed this ayah concerning it.

**Three things the scholars draw from this ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets them out:

1. **The Messenger's permission is called Allah's permission.** Neither cutting nor sparing was an explicit command of Allah. Apparently what each group did was on the basis of independent reasoning (*ijtihād*); at most, they may have sought the permission of the Prophet ﷺ — which is Hadith, not Qur'an. Yet the Qur'an calls it *bi-idhni-llāh*, "with Allah's permission." Allah has given His Messenger ﷺ the right to legislate laws, which lines up with ayah 7 of this surah, that believers must hold fast to what the Messenger ﷺ gives them and abstain from what he forbids. This shows conclusively that the Sunnah is an independent source of Islamic law.

2. **Disagreement in ijtihād is not sin.** Two groups of Companions reached opposite conclusions and Allah endorsed both. If those competent to undertake *ijtihād* (independent legal reasoning) differ, so that one holds a thing permissible and the other impermissible, neither is counted sinful, nor does the principle of *nahy ʿan al-munkar* (forbidding evil) apply between them — because neither of the two rulings is an evil in Allah's sight.

3. **The ruling itself.** Is it legitimate to demolish or burn the homes of hostile unbelievers, cut or burn their trees, or destroy their fields and farms? The leading authorities on Islamic jurisprudence are not unanimous. Imam Abu Hanifah ruled all of these permitted. Shaykh Ibn al-Humam qualified and restricted it: permitted only where the enemy cannot otherwise be vanquished, or where the victory of the Muslims is not probable — the whole purpose being to break the might and power of the enemy (Mazhari). And the ayah's closing words set the intention: *"so that He might disgrace the rebellious"* — which is why, as Maʿārif explains, the cutting and burning here cannot be construed as disorderliness in the earth.

## What this asks of us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the restraint in the episode, striking given a tribe that repeatedly plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ: even when their treacheries reached their peak, no massacre was contemplated and no thought of seizing their property was ever considered. They were ordered only to evacuate the town; even after some trees were cut and burned, no edict was issued to burn down their fortresses or attack them; and no Muslim ever frowned upon any of them as he carried his things out. All of this at a moment when they were completely subdued and the Prophet ﷺ was in complete command, with the power to fully avenge their treachery — and he did not use it. This is exactly how he behaved with the pagans of Makkah when he entered the city after the triumph.

Ayah 2 leaves one command: *fa-ʿtabirū*. Everyone builds fortresses — savings, status, standing, plans. The tribe's walls were real and useless at once, because what came did not come at the walls. And notice where the false confidence came from: ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy's two thousand men who never marched. Promises from people who have no fear of Allah are the thinnest wall of all.

Everything in the heavens and the earth is already glorifying the One who is ʿAzīz and Ḥakīm. To align yourself with Him is to join what the whole of creation is doing already. Ayah 4 names the alternative: *"whosoever opposes Allah, then verily, Allah is Severe in punishment."*

passages.title: Fay': wealth taken without a battle
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat set out the law of *fay'* — wealth that comes to the Muslim community from its enemies without a battle being fought — and then widen out into one of the great principles of Islam: that whatever the Messenger ﷺ gives you, you take, and whatever he forbids you, you leave.

What holds the passage together is a single movement: **Allah is the real owner, the Messenger ﷺ is the trustee, and the community receives on Allah's terms.** Ayah 6 explains why this wealth is not the soldiers' to divide; ayah 7 explains whose it is, why it is distributed the way it is, and what obedience that distribution demands.

## The occasion: Banu an-Nadir, taken without a fight

The immediate case is the Jewish tribe of Banu an-Nadir, whose expulsion the sūrah has just described. Ibn Kathir explains that the Muslims did not fight them in battle at all; **Allah forced them out of their forts on account of the fear He placed in their hearts for Allah's Messenger ﷺ.**

That is exactly what ayah 6 says: *"for this you made no expedition with either cavalry or camelry."* Ibn Kathir glosses *rikāb* here as **referring to using camels**.

Because of that, Ibn Kathir says, **it was *fay'* that Allah awarded His Messenger ﷺ, with his discretion to spend it as he saw fit** — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states below, *fay'* is not divided among the fighters the way battle spoils are.

Then the reason is given at the level of ultimate cause: *"But Allah gives power to His Messengers over whomsoever He wills. And Allah is Able to do all things."* Ibn Kathir comments that this means **Allah is powerful and cannot be resisted or opposed; He is the Compeller over all things.**

## The word *fay'*: wealth that comes back

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the term. **The verb *afā'a* is derived from *fay'un*, which means "to return."** The same word is used for the time of the afternoon **when the shade of things returns to the east**.

Why is confiscated wealth called a "return"? The real ownership of the entire universe belongs to Allah. Human beings own what they own only because Allah, through His Law, declares it theirs. When people rebel against Allah in disbelief and shirk, and their property is confiscated through a properly constituted authority, **that ownership returns to the Real Owner, Allah.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about the translation: *fay'* should not simply be rendered "booty." The Sharīʿah distinguishes two categories:

- **Ghanīmah** — property acquired from non-Muslims *through active armed struggle*. Its rules are laid down in Sūrah al-Anfāl (8:41).
- **Fay'** — property acquired *without* an actual fight: what non-Muslims leave behind and flee from, or make over to the Muslim authority willingly and with consent — including *kharāj*, *jizyah*, or commercial duty, that is, established levies handed over to the authority rather than seized in battle. Its rules are laid down here.

## "From the people of the townships": a general law, not a one-off

Ayah 7 shifts from *"from them"* to *"from the people of the townships"* (*ahl al-qurā*). Ibn Kathir reads this as deliberate generalisation: it means **all the villages and areas that are conquered in this manner** — the wealth collected from them falls under the same ruling as the wealth acquired from Banu an-Nadir. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies "the people of the towns" as the Jewish tribes such as Banu Nadir and Banu Quraizah, whose wealth and property were obtained without armed struggle.

The practical difference from ghanīmah is sharp: **fay' is not distributed among the *mujāhidīn*** — the participants in the fighting. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that the Prophet ﷺ was granted full authority over it — to give as much as he liked to whomever he liked, or to retain it at his discretion — while a few classes of beneficiary were clearly defined, and the distribution had to stay within them.

## Six named, five who receive

*"It is for Allah, His Messenger, the kindred, the orphans, the poor, and the wayfarer."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the wording here is almost identical to the wording for the *khums* (one-fifth) of ghanīmah in 8:41 — the same six classes in the same order. Why begin with Allah, who needs nothing?

The answer given is that **Allah's name is mentioned by way of blessing or benediction** — wealth associated with Allah's name attains honour and distinction, and the mention also points to its permissibility and purity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this view to Sayyidnā Hasan al-Basri, Qatadah, ʿAtā', Ibrāhīm and Shaʿbi, and to the commentators in general (via Mazhari).

**Prophets are not allowed to avail of *sadaqāt* — charities** — even though these come from the pure wealth of the Muslims. So how are ghanīmah and fay' lawful for him ﷺ, when they are derived from those who rejected faith? The mention of Allah's name at the beginning of the verse removes the doubt. When a segment of humanity rebels and jihād is waged against them by Allah's command, their wealth is confiscated in the name of the authority in command — it leaves the ownership of the disbelievers and **is deposited separately as being under the ownership of Allah alone.** No human being has any entitlement to it. The beneficiaries therefore **receive it directly from Allah**, and so it is lawful and pure — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān compares it to water and self-growing grass, a direct Divine gift. It is no sadaqah or khairāt.

That leaves five classes of beneficiary: **the Messenger ﷺ, the kinsmen, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.**

**On the kinsmen.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "kinsmen" means the kinsmen of the Prophet ﷺ, and that they were granted a share for two reasons: first, because they helped him ﷺ and supported him in his Islamic activities — on this basis even his *rich* kinsmen used to be granted a share; second, because sadaqah was unlawful for them, so his poor and needy relatives were provided for out of fay' rather than out of charity. After his ﷺ passing, the first reason no longer existed, so the share of the rich relatives fell into disuse, as did the share of the Prophet ﷺ himself. **The poor and needy among his relatives continued to receive their share** on account of poverty and need, and were given priority over other poor and needy people (from the *Hidāyah*).

**On the authority governing it.** Citing Qurtubi, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that the rules for fay' and for the khums of ghanīmah are identical: both are in the full authority of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and after him in the authority of the Caliphs. The authority may retain them for the benefit of the Muslims in general, or deposit them in the *bayt al-māl* (public treasury) and grant nothing to anyone, or distribute them — and if distribution is chosen, it must be done within the five defined classes.

## How the Prophet ﷺ actually used it

Ibn Kathir reports that **Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿUmar**: the wealth of Banu an-Nadir was of the fay' type that Allah awarded His Messenger ﷺ, and for which the Muslims did not have to use cavalry or camelry. Therefore it was for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — **and he used it for the needs of his family for a year at a time, and the rest was used to buy armour and weapons used in the cause of Allah.** Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad collected the short form of this story, and that the Group, with the exception of Ibn Majah, collected this hadith.

**The scene in ʿUmar's house.** Ibn Kathir then relates a long narration recorded by **Abu Dawud** from Malik bin Aws. Malik is summoned when the sun has risen high and it has grown hot, and finds ʿUmar sitting on a bedstead made of date-palm leaves *and without a mattress* — arranging famine relief for other people's families while sitting on that.

Into that room come ʿUthmān bin ʿAffān, ʿAbdur-Rahmān bin ʿAwf, az-Zubayr bin al-ʿAwwām and Saʿd bin Abi Waqqās, and after them al-ʿAbbās and ʿAli — the latter two asking ʿUmar to judge between them over the Prophet's ﷺ property. ʿUmar puts them all under oath "by Allah by Whose permission the heaven and the earth exist": do you know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said,

> **"Our property will not be inherited. Whatever we leave, is charity"?**

They all confirm it. ʿUmar then says that Allah bestowed on His Messenger ﷺ a special favour unlike what He gave all other people, and recites **this very ayah** — *"And what Allah gave as booty (fay') to His Messenger from them…"* — drawing the conclusion: this property was especially given to Allah's Messenger ﷺ, "however, by Allah, neither did he take possession of it and leave you, nor did he favour himself with it to your exclusion." He took the yearly expenses from it for himself and his family and left the rest in the Muslim Treasury.

ʿUmar then recounts the history: when Allah took His Prophet ﷺ unto Him, Abu Bakr said, "I am the successor of Allah's Messenger ﷺ"; al-ʿAbbās came seeking his share of inheritance from his nephew and ʿAli seeking his wife's share from her father's inheritance, and Abu Bakr answered them with the same hadith. ʿUmar affirms that **Abu Bakr was true, pious, rightly guided and a follower of what was right.** After Abu Bakr died, ʿUmar managed the property as long as Allah allowed him to, then handed it over to the two of them on the pledge that they would manage it in the same way as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to — and now, asked to rule differently, he refuses: "By Allah, I will never give any decision other than what I have already given, until the Last Hour begins." Ibn Kathir notes that they recorded this from the hadith of az-Zuhri.

## "So that it does not become a fortune circulating among the rich"

*Kay lā yakūna dūlatan bayna al-aghniyā'i minkum.* Qurtubi, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, glosses **dūlah** as "wealth or good fortune that exchange hands."

Ibn Kathir's comment is plain: the expenditures for the fay' were made like this **so that the wealth does not remain among the wealthy**, who would spend it as they wish and desire and give none of it to the poor. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the historical edge — the verse is aimed at abolishing an old practice of the Days of Ignorance, in which the circulation of such wealth remained confined to the privileged and propertied class, and the poorer segment of society had no entitlement to the wealth of the nation.

The wealth was not distributed by rank, and not by who fought. It was routed instead to named classes: the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out. Allah has kept the distribution of humanity's most basic needs largely in His own hands, beyond any individual's domination — air, wind, atmosphere, the sun, the moon, the light of the stars and planets, the rain-laden clouds. All natural resources are declared a public endowment for all; not even the greatest sovereign authorities can monopolise them. Islamic law likewise declares hills and mountains, unpopulated jungles and natural springs to be public endowments, while allowing legitimate ownership of some parts of the earth under special laws. Gold, silver and money are not themselves basic needs, but Allah has made them the means of acquiring every essential of life — and it is here that greed produces systems of monopolisation and concentration.

Islam works from both sides. It shows **the highest respect to individual property rights**: a person's lawful property is as sacred and inviolable as human life itself, and under the penal law the hand that steals it is amputated. And it shuts the doors through which wealth pools in a few hands: **usury, speculation, gambling and betting are declared unlawful**, and wealth gained lawfully is given specific ways of spending — Zakāh, ʿUshr, Sadaqat al-Fitr, the various forms of expiation, and voluntary charity from the surplus. At death the estate passes by fixed shares on the principle of *al-aqrab fa'l-aqrab*, "relatives in order of relationship" — the nearer in degree excluding the more remote. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict is blunt: when wealth concentrated in the hands of a few capitalists and people at the helm of affairs, that economic situation gave birth, as a reaction, to such unreasonable systems as communism and socialism — and it calls it unwise and short-sighted to give up Islam's balanced system of economics based on justice, fair play and compassion.

## "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it"

**In its immediate context**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the verse concerns the distribution itself. Allah has set down the beneficiaries of this property, but *how much* each receives was left to the discretion of the Prophet ﷺ. So the Muslims are advised to happily accept the amount he grants them, and not to be anxious to receive what he has not given them. The following words — *"and fear Allah"* — further emphasise this: if anyone collects more than what he is granted under false pretext, Allah is fully aware and will punish him.

**But the wording is general.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that although the verse was revealed in connection with fay', its words are not specific to wealth; they cover the commands as well. Whatever the Prophet ﷺ gives a person — wealth, any other grant, or any command — must be willingly accepted, and whatever he forbids must be stayed away from. **Many of the Companions took the generalised sense of the verse, and on that basis took the Prophet's ﷺ commandment as binding as the Qur'anic commandment.**

**A grammatical clue.** Qurtubi observes that in this verse the antonym of *ātā* ("gives") is *nahā* ("forbids"). This shows that *ātā* is being used in the sense of *amara* ("commands"), which is the direct antonym of *nahā*. The Qur'an employed "gives" rather than the direct opposite, presumably to embrace the subject matter in which the verse occurs — the disbursement of fay'.

Three illustrations:

**1. Ibn Masʿūd and Umm Yaʿqūb.** Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿūd that Allah curses women who practise tattooing and those who get themselves tattooed, and the women who remove the hair from their eyebrows and faces and those who make artificial spaces between their teeth in order to look more beautiful, thereby changing Allah's creation. A woman of Bani Asad called Umm Yaʿqūb came to him and challenged him: she had read the whole Qur'an and did not find in it what he said. He answered, "Why should I not curse those whom Allah's Messenger ﷺ has cursed and who are cursed in Allah's Book!" — and recited this very ayah: *"And whatsoever the Messenger gives you take it and whatsoever he forbids you, you abstain from it."* She admitted she had read it. She then suspected his own wife of these practices; he told her to go and look at her, and she found nothing in support of her claim. He said: if my wife were as you thought, I would not keep her with me. Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Sahihs recorded this from the hadith of Sufyan ath-Thawri.

**A prohibition can be "in Allah's Book" by virtue of this ayah, even when the specific act is not named in it.**

**2. Ibn Masʿūd and the pilgrim in sewn clothes.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that Sayyidnā ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿūd once saw a person in the state of *ihrām* — the sacred state a pilgrim enters, in which wearing sewn, tailored clothes is not permitted — wearing sewn clothes, and asked him to take them off. The man asked him to recite a Qur'anic verse in support of the claim. Ibn Masʿūd recited this very verse.

**3. Imam Shāfiʿī and the wasp.** Imam Shāfiʿī once said to his gathering: ask whatever you wish, and I will answer from the Qur'an. Someone asked about a pilgrim in ihrām who killed a wasp. He recited *"Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it"* and coupled it with a narration giving the injunction relating to that (from Qurtubi).

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith of Abu Hurayrah, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"When I order you to do something, then do as much as you can of it. If I forbid something for you, then shun it."**

## "And have taqwā of Allah; verily Allah is severe in punishment"

Ibn Kathir explains **taqwā** here as fearing Allah by obeying His orders and refraining from His prohibitions — and adds that Allah is severe in punishment for those who defy Him, reject and disobey His commands, and commit what He forbids and prohibits.

## Living it

- **What comes without a fight is not distributed like what was won in one.** Ayah 6 states it plainly: *"for this you made no expedition with either cavalry or camelry."* The wealth is handled on Allah's terms, not the claimants'.
- **Design the outflow, not just the income.** The concern of the verse, as both commentaries read it, is that the wealth *not remain* among the wealthy — that it not settle permanently in the same hands.
- **Take what you are given without eyeing what you were not.** The first application of "whatever the Messenger gives you, take it," on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, was contentment with one's allotted share — and *"fear Allah"* is the warning against claiming more.
- **Accept the Sunnah as binding.** Ibn Masʿūd's answer to Umm Yaʿqūb is the model, and many of the Companions read the verse this way: a command of the Prophet ﷺ is binding as a command of the Qur'an — the Qur'an itself here hands you over to him.

passages.title: Who the fay' belongs to, and why they deserve it
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat name the *people* who receive a share of the *fay'* — and, more strikingly, *why*. Ibn Kathir: Allah states the categories of needy people who also deserve a part of the fay'. But He does not merely list recipients; He describes their character. Ayah 8 gives the Muhajirin, ayah 9 the Ansar, ayah 10 everyone after them until the end of time — three circles widening outward, each earning its place by what is in the heart.

## The first circle: the poor emigrants (ayah 8)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 8 as a portrait in four strokes.

**One: they were driven out.** *Alladhīna ukhrijū min diyārihim wa amwālihim* — "expelled from their homes and their property." Their only crime, Maʿārif notes (citing Mazhari and Qurtubi), was embracing Islam and standing by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; the pagans of Makkah persecuted them until they had to abandon their hearths and homes for Madinah. Some tied stones to their stomachs against unbearable hunger; others dug holes in the ground to shelter from the winter cold. Ibn Kathir adds a second dimension to *ukhrijū*: they "departed their homes and defied their people." Expelled — but they also walked out.

**A legal point in one word.** Allah calls them *al-fuqarā'*, the poor. In Islamic law a *faqīr* has no property at all, or too little to reach the *niṣāb*. Yet most of these emigrants had been wealthy in Makkah; had that wealth still legally been theirs, "poor" would be inaccurate. Maʿārif draws the ruling out of this: Imam Abu Hanifah and Imam Malik ruled that when Muslims abandon homes and possessions and migrate, and non-believers take control of what remains, ownership passes to them — so their sale and purchase of such property is recognised in the Shariah.

**Two: their motive was pure.** *Yabtaghūna faḍlan mina-llāhi wa riḍwānā* — "seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure." Ibn Kathir glosses it as "seeking the acceptance of Allah and His favor." Maʿārif adds a fine distinction: *faḍl* is normally used of worldly blessing, *riḍwān* of the blessings of the Hereafter. So they gave up every comfort they had, and now sought both their worldly needs *and* their eternal ones under the shade of Islam alone.

**Three: they helped Allah and His Messenger.** *Wa yanṣurūna-llāha wa rasūlah.* To "help Allah," Maʿārif explains, means to help His religion — and for it they made staggering sacrifices.

**Four: they are the truthful.** *Ulā'ika humu-ṣ-ṣādiqūn.* Ibn Kathir: they were "truthful in statement and deed, and they are the chiefs of the Muhajirin." Maʿārif presses further: they made a covenant with Allah and His Messenger when they pronounced the *kalimah*, and proved true to it. The ayah is thus an open testimony from Allah to the truthfulness of the emigrant Companions — so to call any of them a liar is to reject the ayah itself. Maʿārif notes (citing al-Baghawi and Mazhari) that the Prophet ﷺ held them in such esteem that he would supplicate through their *wasīlah*.

## The second circle: those who were already there (ayah 9)

*Wa-lladhīna tabawwa'u-d-dāra wal-īmāna min qablihim.* Ibn Kathir: this refers to those already living in the city of the Hijrah before the emigrants arrived, and who accepted faith before many of them did — the Ansar.

**A beautiful grammatical knot.** *Tabawwa'a* means to take up dwelling in a place. But the ayah couples two objects to it: "the abode **and** faith." A house can be settled into; faith is not a place. Maʿārif reports two resolutions. Some scholars hold an implied verb governs the second noun — *akhlaṣū* or *tamakkanū* — giving "they settled in their abode and became sincere and firmly established in faith." Others take *īmān* metaphorically: faith itself is the fortified house they moved into for refuge. Either way, the phrase makes their belief sound like an address, somewhere they lived.

*Min qablihim*, "before them," carries its own honour: they were established in Madinah first — a city so central that the Muslims of Makkah were commanded to migrate to it. Maʿārif records (citing Qurtubi) that Imam Malik regarded Madinah as the most distinguished of all cities on one ground: every city Islam reached, Makkah included, was opened by *jihād* — Madinah alone was opened by *īmān*.

**They loved the arrivals.** *Yuḥibbūna man hājara ilayhim.* The emigrants reached Madinah stripped of everything. Maʿārif observes how unnatural the response was: normally no community is willing to take in so large a number of destitute newcomers. The Ansar received them with open arms and made them equal partners in what they owned — so eagerly that each emigrant drew several Ansari claimants, and lots often had to be cast. Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas that the Muhajirin said, "We have never met people like those whom we emigrated to; comforting us in times of scarcity and giving us with a good heart in times of abundance... we feared that they might earn the whole reward instead of us." He ﷺ answered that they would not, so long as the emigrants thanked them and made du'a for them.

## The night the fay' was divided

The Muhajirin at that point had no homes and no property; they lived in Ansari houses and worked Ansari farms. When the wealth of Banu Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa' came in as *fay'*, the Prophet ﷺ summoned the leader of the Ansar, Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and told him to bring all the tribes of the Ansar. Then he set out two options: divide the wealth between Muhajirin and Ansar, with the emigrants staying on as usual in Ansari homes — or give all of it to the homeless emigrants, who would then move out and settle in homes of their own.

Two of the chiefs of the Ansar, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, stood up: give the entire *fay'* to our emigrant brothers, and let them go on living in our homes as well. Every one of the Ansar concurred. The Prophet ﷺ supplicated for them and their children, and distributed the whole of the *fay'* among the Muhajirin. Only two of the Ansar received a grant from it, because they were very poor — Sahl ibn Hunayf and Abu Dujanah; and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was given a sword, the distinguished sword of Ibn Abi'l-Huqayq. (Maʿārif reports this from Mazhari, who cites *Subul al-Rashād* of Muhammad ibn Yusuf as-Salihi.)

This is the background to *wa lā yajidūna fī ṣudūrihim ḥājatan mimmā ūtū* — "they find in their breasts no need for what has been given to them." Ibn Kathir explains it as the absence of envy over the higher status Allah gave the Muhajirin; Qatadah and Ibn Zayd say "what they have been given" refers to what the Muhajirin were favoured with. Maʿārif reads *ḥājah* as "any item of need": whatever the emigrants received, the Ansar accepted as though they had no need of any of it.

The same spirit surfaced later. Al-Bukhari recorded from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ called the Ansar to divide al-Bahrayn among them, and they refused — "not until you give a similar portion to our emigrant brothers." He ﷺ replied that they would soon see others preferred over them, so they should be patient until they met him on the Day of Resurrection.

And the debt was repaid. Maʿārif notes that self-sacrifice cannot run in one direction only — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged Muslims to exchange gifts and so increase their mutual love, and one who receives should return the favour with wealth if Allah has given him wealth, and with du'a if not. Az-Zuhri reports from Anas that when the Prophet ﷺ returned from the expedition of Khaybar, the emigrants — all of them — worked out every gift the Ansar had made them and gave it back.

## Īthār: the word at the heart of the passage

*Wa yu'thirūna 'alā anfusihim wa law kāna bihim khaṣāṣah* — "they give preference to others over themselves, even though poverty is theirs." *Īthār*, Maʿārif explains, is putting another's wish, need and desire above your own; *khaṣāṣah* is poverty. Ibn Kathir: they began with other people before themselves, though they too were in need.

Ibn Kathir marks how high this rank is by setting it against two other Qur'anic descriptions — those who "give food, in spite of their love for it" (76:8) and give "wealth, in spite of love for it" (2:177). Those give while loving what they give, but not while *needing* it; these give what they have a necessity for. He cites an authentic hadith that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The best charity is that given when one is in need and struggling," and relates that Abu Bakr as-Siddiq gave away all his wealth, and when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked what he had left for his family, said, "I kept for them Allah and His Messenger."

**The night the lamp went out.** Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ saying poverty had struck him. The Prophet ﷺ sent to his wives and they had nothing, so he asked, "Who will host this man tonight — may Allah grant His mercy to him who does so?" An Ansari man volunteered, took him home, and told his wife to honour the guest of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ generously. She said, "By Allah, we have nothing except the meal for my children." He said: let the children sleep if they ask for supper, then turn off the lamp, and we will go to bed hungry. She did as he asked. In the morning the Prophet ﷺ told him that Allah had wondered at — or laughed at — what he and his wife had done. Then this part of the ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir adds that Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i also collected this hadith, and that in another narration the Companion is named as Abu Talhah al-Ansari.

Maʿārif, following Qurtubi, gathers other incidents of the same spirit: 'A'ishah, fasting, giving away her only loaf to a poor man — and being sent that evening a roasted goat, at which she told her maid, "This is better than that bread of yours" (*Muwaṭṭa'* of Imam Malik). And at Yarmuk, Ibn Kathir records, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and two other wounded men each sent the sip of water on to the next; all three died and none of them drank. Maʿārif carries a fuller version of the Yarmuk account from Hudhayfah al-'Adawi, in which the water passes among seven of the dying and reaches none of them in time.

Maʿārif then raises the obvious objection: the Prophet ﷺ discouraged giving away *all* one's wealth — a man once brought a piece of gold about the size of an egg to give in charity, and he ﷺ threw it back towards him, saying that some bring all their wealth to give away, then become poor and go about begging. Maʿārif answers that people's conditions differ, and so the rulings differ. The prohibition addresses one who gives all, then regrets it, cannot endure the poverty, and begs. For one who gives all and meets it with calm courage and resolute endurance — as Abu Bakr did, and having raised his family to face life the same way, so no one's rights are usurped — it is permitted.

**And whoever is saved from the greed of his soul.** *Wa man yūqa shuḥḥa nafsihī fa-ulā'ika humu-l-mufliḥūn.* Maʿārif notes that ayah 9 closes on a universal principle. *Shuḥḥ* and *bukhl* (miserliness) are near-synonyms, but *shuḥḥ* carries the sense of intense craving for money and possessions. Both are absolutely forbidden where they stop a person fulfilling obligatory rights — rights of Allah such as zakah, sadaqat al-fitr and 'ushr, or rights of people such as maintaining family, needy parents and relatives. Where they merely block laudable, rewardable spending it is reprehensible; declining merely customary spending is not *shuḥḥ* in the Shariah's sense.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Be on your guard against oppression, for oppression is a darkness on the Day of Resurrection. And be on your guard against being stingy, for being stingy destroyed those who were before you — it made them shed blood and make lawful what was unlawful for them." Muslim collected this hadith.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Aswad ibn Hilal that a man came to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in fear: "I fear that I have earned destruction for myself" — for he had heard this ayah, "and I am somewhat a miser who barely gives away anything." 'Abdullah answered that this is not the greed Allah mentions in the Qur'an, which pertains to illegally consuming your brother's wealth. "What you have is miserliness, and it is an evil thing indeed to be a miser."

Maʿārif closes ayah 9 with the narration Ibn Kathir cites from Imam Ahmad, from Anas: three days running the Prophet ﷺ said "a man is about to arrive who is from among the inmates of Paradise," and each time the same Ansari came in, water of wudu dripping from his beard, his shoes in his left hand. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As contrived to stay three nights in his house to learn his secret, and found nothing remarkable — no rising for tahajjud, only some dhikr of Allah as he lay down, and in three days not a single word from him but good. Asked outright, the man said: "I have no deed more than what you have seen." Then he called him back: "Yes — there is something. I harbour in my heart no malice or evil against any Muslim, and I am not jealous or envious of any Muslim for anything good Allah has given him." Ibn Kathir notes that An-Nasa'i cites it too, in *'Amal al-Yawm wal-Laylah*, with a chain authentic by the standard of al-Bukhari and Muslim.

## The third circle: everyone after (ayah 10)

*Wa-lladhīna jā'ū min ba'dihim yaqūlūna...* Ibn Kathir calls this the third type of believer whose poor most deserve a part of the *fay'*: the Muhajirin, the Ansar, and those who followed their righteous lead with excellence — the same three named in 9:100.

Maʿārif draws out a striking legal consequence: this ayah lays down that all Muslims until the Last Hour, after the Muhajirin and Ansar, are entitled to a share in *fay'* wealth. That, Maʿārif reports (transmitted by Malik and Qurtubi), is why 'Umar al-Faruq did not divide the conquered lands of Iraq, Syria and Egypt among the fighters, but retained them as a public endowment for coming generations, its income accruing to the Muslim treasury. Questioned by Companions, he cited this ayah: were it not for the Muslims yet to come, he would have divided every territory as it fell, as the Prophet ﷺ had done with the lands of Khaybar — but if the present generation takes it all, nothing is left for those after.

**What is asked of us.** The mark of this third group is not migration, not sheltering the homeless — they came too late for either. Just a du'a: *Rabbanā-ghfir lanā wa li-ikhwāninā-lladhīna sabaqūnā bil-īmān wa lā taj'al fī qulūbinā ghillan lilladhīna āmanū* — "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put not in our hearts any rancour toward those who believed." Ibn Kathir glosses *ghill* as rage or envy. So the whole contribution of the later Ummah, as Maʿārif frames it, is to recognise the high station of the Muhajirin and Ansar — they preceded us in faith and were the means by which it reached us — to pray for the forgiveness of all, and to ask that our own hearts be cleansed of bitterness and spite toward true and sincere Muslims.

Maʿārif states the implication plainly: for the validity and acceptance of the faith of every generation after the Companions, it is a necessary condition that they love and respect the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and pray for the believers who went before. When a man questioned Husayn about 'Uthman, Husayn asked: are you of the Muhajirin? No. Of the Ansar? No. "Then only the third ayah remains — and if you wish to cast doubt on 'Uthman, you will have to leave that category too."

Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Malik reasoned beautifully from this ayah that the Rafidah who curse the Companions have no share in *fay'* wealth, since they lack the very quality Allah describes here. Maʿārif reports the argument in more detail: Qurtubi says this ayah proves that love of the Companions is obligatory; and Imam Malik argues from this ayah that every Muslim has a share in *fay'*, so that whoever has none, his faith in Islam is doubtful.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that 'A'ishah said of such people, "They were commanded to invoke Allah to forgive them, but instead they cursed them!" — and recited this ayah. Ibn 'Abbas observed that Allah commanded Muslims to pray for the Companions and seek forgiveness for them *knowing* that conflicts and civil wars would occur among them; so it is not permissible for any Muslim to hold evil thoughts about them on account of those conflicts.

**The ayah does not stop at avoiding hatred; it teaches you to ask Allah to remove it.** *Lā taj'al fī qulūbinā ghillā* is a request — the heart is not assumed to be automatically clean. And the du'a ends where it must: *Rabbanā innaka Ra'ūfun Raḥīm* — "Our Lord, You are indeed full of kindness, Most Merciful." Two of Allah's beautiful names, placed exactly where someone who has just asked for a purified heart would need them.

## Living it

The passage names three qualities and asks whether you have them. The Muhajirin's is sincerity when everything has been taken from you — seeking only *faḍl* and *riḍwān*. The Ansar's is *īthār*: not merely giving, but giving first, out of what you needed. And the third circle's is a clean chest — the Ansari of Paradise whose only secret was that he envied no Muslim anything Allah had given him. That last one is open to anyone, on any night, for the cost of a du'a and the refusal to nurse a grudge.

passages.title: The hypocrites' hollow pledge of support
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The sūrah has been recounting the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banū an-Naḍīr. In ayat 11–14 the camera turns away from the fortresses and onto a quieter set of actors: the hypocrites, who had promised Banū an-Naḍīr that they would stand with them against the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Ibn Kathir titles this section exactly that — "The False Promise of Support the Hypocrites gave to the Jews."

The four ayat move as one piece. Ayah 11 quotes the promise word for word and Allah Himself testifies that it is a lie. Ayah 12 takes the promise apart clause by clause and shows exactly how it will fail. Ayat 13 and 14 then explain *why* it was empty from the beginning: hearts that fear people more than they fear Allah, and an alliance that looks solid from outside but is fractured within. Each of the two explanations closes with a "because" — and the two "becauses" are not identical, as we will see.

## The moment behind the words

Ibn Kathir reports that the hypocrites — **ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy and his like** — sent a messenger to Banū an-Naḍīr promising them help. That single detail changes how the passage reads. This is not only a general character sketch of hypocrisy; it is a specific message, carried by a specific envoy, to a specific people.

So when Allah exposes the promise as worthless, He is not merely correcting the record. He is telling us what that promise was actually made of. The verses open with **أَلَمْ تَرَ** ("Have you not observed…?") — a form of address that invites the listener to look at something and see it for what it is. What passed between the hypocrites and Banū an-Naḍīr is put on public display.

## Ayah 11: a promise made in the strongest words Arabic has

Read the quoted promise slowly, because much of its force is in how it is worded:

- **لَئِنْ أُخْرِجْتُمْ لَنَخْرُجَنَّ مَعَكُمْ** — "If you are expelled, we indeed will go out with you." The verb carries the emphatic *lām* and the doubled *nūn* of emphasis (*la-nakhrujanna*) — in Arabic, this is the register of swearing on something. Notice too that both verbs are built on the same root, *kh-r-j* (going out): *ukhrijtum* / *la-nakhrujanna*. Whatever going-out is decreed for you, they say, is the going-out we take upon ourselves.
- **وَلَا نُطِيعُ فِيكُمْ أَحَدًا أَبَدًا** — "and we shall never obey anyone against you." **أَبَدًا** (*abadan*, "ever") closes off every future exception.
- **وَإِنْ قُوتِلْتُمْ لَنَنْصُرَنَّكُمْ** — "and if you are attacked, we shall indeed help you." Again the same double emphasis.

Three pledges, each maximally strong: we will share your exile, we will never take a side against you, we will fight for you. No one talks like this unless they want to be believed absolutely.

**"Their brothers."** Allah calls Banū an-Naḍīr **إِخْوَانِهِمُ** — "their brethren" — while at the same time identifying them as **الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ**, "those who disbelieved from the People of the Scripture." A brotherhood is real here, but it is not the brotherhood of faith the sūrah has been praising in the Muhājirīn and the Anṣār just before this passage. The word choice is quietly devastating: whatever these men professed with their tongues, Allah is telling us where their loyalty actually lay.

**"But Allah is Witness that they verily are liars."** Then comes **وَاللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ إِنَّهُمْ لَكَاذِبُونَ**. Human beings judge oaths by how emphatic they sound. Allah judges them by what is inside the one who swears. Ibn Kathir explains this in two layers:

1. **They lied when they issued the promise** — "it was just words that they did not intend to fulfill." The intention to keep it was never there.
2. **Even if they had meant it**, "what they said they would do, would never have been fulfilled by them." Their nature would not have carried them through.

So the promise was false twice over: false in the heart at the moment it was spoken, and false in the outcome it could never have produced. Ibn Kathir explicitly connects this second layer to what comes next — "and this is why Allah said" — moving straight from Allah's testimony in ayah 11 to the detailed answer in ayah 12.

## Ayah 12: the promise dismantled, clause by clause

Ayah 12 answers ayah 11 point for point, in the same order, and adds one more collapse the hypocrites had not even considered:

- **لَئِنْ أُخْرِجُوا لَا يَخْرُجُونَ مَعَهُمْ** — "Surely, if they are expelled, never will they go out with them." Pledge one, cancelled.
- **وَلَئِنْ قُوتِلُوا لَا يَنْصُرُونَهُمْ** — "and if they are attacked, they will never help them." Ibn Kathir: "the hypocrites will not fight along with the Jews." Pledge two, cancelled.
- **وَلَئِنْ نَصَرُوهُمْ لَيُوَلُّنَّ الْأَدْبَارَ ثُمَّ لَا يُنْصَرُونَ** — "And even if they do help them, they will turn their backs, and they will not be victorious." Ibn Kathir: "even if the hypocrites did fight along their side," this is where it would end.

Look at what that last clause does. Allah does not merely say the help will not come; He follows the hypothetical all the way through. *Suppose* they showed up. *Suppose* they took the field. They would still break and run — **لَيُوَلُّنَّ الْأَدْبَارَ**, "they will turn their backs" — and then, having fled, they themselves would not be helped. It is worth noticing the wording: the same root the hypocrites used in their pledge of victory, *n-ṣ-r* (*la-nanṣurannakum*, "we shall indeed help you"), returns at the end of the clause in the passive — *lā yunṣarūn*, "they will not be helped." The would-be helpers end as the ones nobody helps.

**This is good news.** Ibn Kathir pauses here to say something the reader can easily miss: *"This Ayah contains good news"* — and he adds that the ayah following it carries good news too. To a believer facing what looks like a coalition of Banū an-Naḍīr plus a hidden faction of allies, Allah is saying: this alliance will not hold, and if it ever does take the field it will collapse. Ibn Kathir records what became of the promise: "When matters got serious and the Jews were besieged, the hypocrites betrayed them and abandoned them to taste utter defeat."

## Ayah 13: the fear is real — it is just pointed the wrong way

**لَأَنْتُمْ أَشَدُّ رَهْبَةً فِي صُدُورِهِمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ** — "Verily, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct: "the hypocrites fear you more than they fear Allah." And he brings a sister verse to show this is a settled pattern of that character: **إِذَا فَرِيقٌ مِنْهُمْ يَخْشَوْنَ النَّاسَ كَخَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ أَوْ أَشَدَّ خَشْيَةً** — "Behold! a section of them fear men as they fear Allah or even more" (4:77).

Two things are worth pausing on. First, the fear is located **فِي صُدُورِهِمْ**, "in their breasts" — not in their words or their posture. The Qur'an is reporting on the inside of a chest, which is precisely what no envoy, no ally, and no enemy could ever verify. That is the same divine knowledge that stands behind the testimony in ayah 11.

Second, this speaks to the failure of the promise. A person who genuinely feared Allah above all else could keep a hard oath, because his ultimate accounting is with One he cannot escape. A person whose deepest dread is directed at people will always calculate: *what can they do to me today?* Such a person's pledges are only as durable as his estimate of the odds.

**"Because they are a people who comprehend not"** — **ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ**. The verb here is from *fiqh* — not, in this context, the technical science of law, but its underlying sense: grasping a thing deeply, perceiving what lies beneath the surface. They can see the strength in front of them; what they do not perceive is the One in whose hand that strength, and they themselves, actually are. That failure of perception is what the ayah names as the reason for the misplaced fear.

## Ayah 14: walls on the outside, cracks on the inside

**لَا يُقَاتِلُونَكُمْ جَمِيعًا إِلَّا فِي قُرًى مُحَصَّنَةٍ أَوْ مِنْ وَرَاءِ جُدُرٍ** — "They fight not against you even together, except in fortified townships, or from behind walls."

Ibn Kathir: "they will not fight Muslims except from behind besieged fortified forts, because of their cowardice and fear of Muslims. They only fight when they have to defend themselves" — even though, he adds, they threaten the Muslims with reprisals. The picture is exact and a little pitiful: loud threats issued from inside a fortress they dare not step outside of. Note the word **جَمِيعًا**, "even together": not even their combined strength changes the calculation.

Then the diagnosis moves from their walls to their hearts, in three quick strokes:

**بَأْسُهُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ شَدِيدٌ** — "Their enmity among themselves is very great." Ibn Kathir: "the enmity they feel against each other is intense." Their ferocity is not absent; it is simply spent on one another. He sets beside it **وَيُذِيقَ بَعْضَكُمْ بَأْسَ بَعْضٍ**, "And make you to taste the violence of one another" (6:65), where the same word *baʾs* carries that mutual savagery.

**تَحْسَبُهُمْ جَمِيعًا وَقُلُوبُهُمْ شَتَّىٰ** — "You would think they were united, but their hearts are divided." The verb **تَحْسَبُ** means *you reckon, you suppose* — it names the observer's impression and corrects it in the same breath. Ibn Kathir: "even though one might see them combining forces and think that these forces are harmonious, yet in reality, they are divided severely." **شَتَّىٰ** (*shattā*) describes things scattered and going in different directions — the opposite of *jamīʿan*, "all together." The outward count says one army; the inward count says a crowd of separate men.

**Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī** said that this ayah refers to the hypocrites and the People of the Scriptures — that is, the "unity" being punctured here is precisely the alliance the passage opened with. The promise of ayah 11 was the seam, and Allah is showing us that the seam was never stitched.

**"Because they are a people who understand not"** — **ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ**. This closing uses a different word from ayah 13's *lā yafqahūn*. Ayah 13 ended with a failure of *fiqh*, deep perception — they could not see past the visible to Allah. Ayah 14 ends with a failure of *ʿaql*, the plain reasoning that ties cause to consequence. A people who reasoned soundly would know that an alliance held together by nothing but common hostility cannot survive contact with real danger.

## Living it

**Measure a promise by the fear behind it, not the emphasis in front of it.** The hypocrites' oath was the most emphatic speech in the passage and the emptiest. Ayah 13 tells you what to look for instead: whom does this person actually fear? A commitment resting on fear of Allah survives a change in circumstances; a commitment resting on fear of people survives only until the circumstances change.

**Audit your own oaths.** Ibn Kathir's first layer — "just words that they did not intend to fulfill" — is a mirror worth holding up. Casual promises made to end a conversation, offers of help extended because the moment called for warmth, commitments to Allah made in a hard week: Allah's testimony in ayah 11 falls exactly on the gap between what the tongue says and what the heart intends, and He witnesses that gap in us too.

**Do not be impressed by appearances of strength.** *Taḥsabuhum jamīʿan* — "you would think they were united." Ayah 14 warns the believer against reading the outward display of an opposing force as the truth about it, and equally against measuring his own community by headcount. What binds hearts is not a shared enemy.

**And take the reassurance.** Ibn Kathir called ayah 12 good news, and it still is. When falsehood assembles a coalition against the truth and it looks formidable, this passage says: look closer. The walls are real. The unity is not.

passages.title: Two similitudes for a divided people
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close the Qur'an's portrait of the hypocrites of Madinah with two comparisons laid side by side, both opening with the same word — *ka-mathal*, "like the likeness of." First a comparison drawn from recent history (ayah 15), then one drawn from the unseen world (ayah 16), and then a single verdict that gathers both parties into one end (ayah 17). What holds them together is a single idea: **the one who whispers you into ruin will not be standing beside you when the ruin arrives.**

## Where we are in the surah

Just before this, in ayat 11–14, Allah exposed a promise. Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites — 'Abdullah bin Ubayy and his like — sent a messenger to Bani An-Nadir promising them help: *"If you are expelled, we indeed will go out with you, and we shall never obey anyone against you; and if you are attacked, we shall indeed help you."* Allah answered that promise before it was ever tested: *"But Allah is Witness that they verily are liars"* (11).

Ibn Kathir gives two reasons why this counted as a lie. First, *"it was just words that they did not intend to fulfill."* And second, *"what they said they would do, would never have been fulfilled by them."* Hence ayah 12: they will not go out with them, they will not help them, and *even if* they did help them, *"they will turn their backs, and they will not be victorious."* Of that verse Ibn Kathir simply says: *"This Ayah contains good news."*

Then the diagnosis. *"Verily, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah"* (13) — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, that the hypocrites fear you more than they fear Allah; he sets it beside *"Behold! a section of them fear men as they fear Allah or even more"* (4:77). And it is because of this, Ibn Kathir notes, that Allah then says *"That is because they are a people who comprehend not."*

They will not fight in the open, only *"in fortified townships, or from behind walls"* (14) — because of their cowardice and fear of the Muslims. And though they look like a bloc, *"you would think they were united, but their hearts are divided."* Ibn Kathir: one might see them combining forces and think those forces harmonious, yet in reality they are divided severely. Ibrahim An-Nakha'i said this ayah refers to the hypocrites and the People of the Scripture. That is the divided people the next ayat address.

## Ayah 15 — "like those just before them"

*"They are like their immediate predecessors; they tasted the evil result of their conduct, and for them a painful torment."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase *"those who were before them in near past."* The reference is not to the ruined nations of antiquity but to something recent.

**Who exactly is meant?** The commentaries record more than one answer.

- Ibn Kathir says it refers to the Jewish tribe of **Bani Qaynuqa'**, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Muhammad bin Ishaq.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it refers to the case of Banu Nadir, and reports that **Mujahid** understood the phrase to mean the **Quraysh of Makkah**, who sustained an ignominious defeat at Badr, while Sayyidna 'Abdullah Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean **Banu Qaynuqa'**, punished for their mischief and machinations after Badr.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then notes what lets more than one answer stand: Banu Nadir were banished after Badr and Uhud, and Banu Qaynuqa' had been banished after Badr; since both the pagans of Makkah and Banu Qaynuqa' faced a deterrent punishment after Badr, both can be the purport of *"those who were before them in the near past ... who tasted the evil consequence of their conduct."*

Notice the verb: they **tasted** it. Not "heard of it" — tasted. And the sentence does not stop at this world: *"and for them a painful torment"* — the worldly humiliation was not the whole account.

## The Banu Qaynuqa' account

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells it in full under this ayah.

When the Prophet ﷺ migrated from Makkah and settled in Madinah, he concluded a peace treaty with the Jewish tribes of the city and its neighbourhood. One of its conditions stipulated that they would not fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims, or assist their enemies. Banu Qaynuqa' were party to that agreement — and were the first to break the pledged word, within a few months.

On the occasion of the battle of Badr they connived with the Quraysh of Makkah, and some incidents of that connivance came out in the open. On that occasion, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, this verse was revealed: *"And if you apprehend a breach from a people, then, throw [the treaty] towards them being right forward"* (8:58). Since Banu Qaynuqa' had, through their treachery, already broken the treaty, the Prophet ﷺ declared war on them. The banner of jihad was given into the hands of Sayyidna Hamzah, Sayyidna Abu Lubabah was appointed deputy in the city of Madinah, and the Prophet ﷺ himself joined the fighting force.

Having seen the Muslim army, they shut themselves up in the fortress. The Prophet ﷺ laid siege to it for fifteen days, and they had no choice but to surrender. Allah cast terror into their hearts; they realised that fighting would not pay off, opened the gate, and expressed their willingness to abide by the Prophet's ﷺ decision.

His ﷺ decision was that the men be executed. **But 'Abdullah Ibn 'Ubayy, the hypocrite, intervened and pleaded with the Prophet ﷺ to pardon them.** In the end it was decided that they should leave and go into exile, their belongings becoming the spoils falling to the lot of the Muslims. They left Madinah and settled in an area called Adhraʿāt in Syria. In compliance with the law of spoils, one-fifth was retained for the *Bait-ul-māl*, the public treasury — after Badr, this was the first one-fifth so retained — and the rest was disbursed among the fighters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dates the incident to Monday, 15th Shawwāl, in the 2nd year of Hijrah: twenty months after the migration.

**Hold two names together.** The man who pleaded for Banu Qaynuqa' is the same 'Abdullah Ibn 'Ubayy whom Ibn Kathir names as sending the messenger to Bani An-Nadir with promises of help. The pattern of the surah's warning is right there in one man's career — and it is worth asking, of any such patron, what his word was actually worth when it came due.

## Ayah 16 — the second comparison: Shaytan

*"Like Shaytan, when he says to man: 'Disbelieve.' But when he disbelieves, Shaytan says: 'I am free of you, I fear Allah, the Lord of all that exists!'"*

Ibn Kathir maps the comparison point for point. The Jews were deceived by the promises of the hypocrites, who said they would help them if the Muslims fought them — and that is the example of the devil. When matters got serious and the Jews were besieged, the hypocrites betrayed them and abandoned them to taste utter defeat. Likewise the devil lures mankind into disbelief, and when they obey him he disowns them and declares himself free of their actions, saying: *"I fear Allah, the Lord of all that exists!"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words: the Shaitan incited man to disbelieve and promised him the world, but when the man was seriously involved in disbelief, he said he had nothing to do with him. Ibn Kathir renders the disavowal *"I am free of you"*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it *"I disown you."* Either way it is the language of a man walking away from a contract. And the excuse offered is grotesque in its piety: the one who commanded the crime pleads that *he* fears Allah — a fear that surfaces only at the moment it can no longer help anyone.

**A recorded instance.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that only Allah knows how many such episodes the devil must have been involved in, but that one such episode is narrated in the Qur'an, in Sūrah al-Anfāl: *"And when the Shaitan beautified their deeds for them and said, 'None of the people is to overpower you today, and I am a protector for you.' But, when the two groups saw each other, he turned back on his heels and said, 'I have nothing to do with you. I am seeing what you do not see. I am scared of Allah, and Allah is severe in punishment'"* (8:48).

That incident, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, occurred on the occasion of the battle of Badr, when the Shaitan misled the pagan Quraysh, urged them to wage war against the Muslims, then withdrew and left them in the lurch in the middle of a pitched battle. How exactly he did it — whether he cast suggestions into their minds or came to them in human shape and spoke to them face to face — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says is not clear, and refers the reader to its fuller discussion in Volume 4. Note the sequence inside the verse itself: *"I am a protector for you"* first, *"I have nothing to do with you"* second. The guarantee and the disavowal come from the same mouth.

**A question the scholars raise.** If the ayah is drawn from that Badr episode, there is a difficulty: the Quraysh were already disbelievers, so in what sense did the Shaitan tell them "Disbelieve"? What he asked of them was that they be firm in opposing the Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the answer is all too obvious: it is all the same whether he asks them to commit kufr, or bids them remain firm in the kufr they are in, or urges them to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — because that too is tantamount to kufr.

**How the trap is actually built.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Tafsir Mazhari, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and others have cited several incidents where monks and devotees were deceived into kufr. In one, an Israelite monk devoted himself to Allah in his synagogue, fasting consecutively and breaking his fast only once in ten days, and spent seventy years of his life this way. Shaytan sent after him the most cunning devil in the shape of a monk, who exerted himself in worship alongside him until he had built up the true worshipper's confidence, then succeeded in teaching him a few prayers efficacious in curing the sick. The devil would then make people fall ill and give them the monk's address; when the monk recited, the devil would remove his influence and they would feel cured. This went on for a long time — until the devil worked on the beautiful daughter of an Israelite leader and sent her too. Step by step the monk was brought to fornication with her; she fell pregnant; the suggestion came that she be killed to save face; and after the killing the devil himself went around telling the story and turned the people against him. In their fury they demolished the synagogue and decided to kill him. Then the Shaitan came back to the monk and told him there was no way to save his life — except one: *"you prostrate to me and I will save your life."* Having already been walked through every other sin, he prostrated. At that point the Shaitan told him plainly: *"I adopted all these guiles for you to commit kufr. I cannot assist you in any way."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the story is recounted fully in Tafsir Mazhari and Qurtubi, and closes it with, "Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best!"

This is not a report from the Prophet ﷺ; the commentators pass it on from earlier sources, and the closing formula is itself a caution. But its lesson is exactly the ayah's: seventy years of worship, and the ruin came not through an open call to disbelief but through a chain of small compliances, each one making the next easier — and at the end, the one who arranged it all steps back and says, *I cannot assist you in any way.*

## Ayah 17 — one end for both

*"So, the end of both will be that they will be in the Fire, abiding therein. Such is the recompense of the wrongdoers."*

The ayah counts them as a pair — *the end of both*. Ibn Kathir states it directly: the end of both, of Shaytan who commanded that disbelief be committed and of those who accepted his call, was the fire of Hell forever. The tempter and the tempted; the hypocrite and the one who trusted him. All the daylight the deceiver put between himself and his victim — *I am free of you* — collapses at the destination. They arrive together.

And then the closing clause widens beyond the case in hand. *"Such is the recompense of the wrongdoers"* — Ibn Kathir: this is the recompense of every unjust person. The passage began with named men in a named year and ends with a rule that outlives them.

## Living it

**Test promises before you spend anything on them.** Ibn Kathir gives two reasons the hypocrites' pledge was a lie: it was just words they did not intend to fulfil, and what they said they would do would never have been fulfilled by them. Banu Nadir staked a tribe on it. Ask of any alliance that asks you to defy Allah: what happens to me if this promise is not kept?

**Look at what happened recently, not only long ago.** Ayah 15 points to those who went before *"in the near past"* — the commentaries name people and a battle within living memory of the first listeners. Allah is teaching a habit of attention: what became of the last people who took this road?

**Distrust the voice that flatters you into risk.** Ibn Kathir's parallel is the whole warning, and 8:48 shows the shape of it: encouragement first, disavowal second. Whoever is loudest that you cannot lose is the least likely to be there when you do.

**And notice the small compliances.** The worshipper in that story was not asked to prostrate to Shaytan on day one. Sin is rarely offered whole; it is offered in instalments.

**Finally, the diagnosis in ayah 13 is the one to fear in yourself:** fearing people more than Allah. Ibn Kathir explains the ayah to mean that the hypocrites feared the believers more than they feared Allah — and it is on the heels of that, he notes, that Allah says *"That is because they are a people who comprehend not."*

passages.title: What every soul sends ahead
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat turn the sūrah inward. The earlier parts of Sūrat al-Ḥashr described events relating to the Jews, the pagans and the hypocrites, and their punishments in this world and in the next; now, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the concluding part of the sūrah makes the believers conscious of their duty toward Allah and advises them to perform righteous deeds regularly. So Allah turns to the believers themselves: be mindful of Him, and look at what you have sent ahead for "tomorrow."

The four ayat run together: a command to be conscious of Allah and to look at what you have sent forward (18), a warning against the opposite condition — forgetting Allah until He makes you forget your own self (19), the declaration that the two destinations are never equal (20), and then an image of what this Book is worthy of doing to a heart — a mountain humbled and split apart under it (21).

## "Tomorrow" — one small word doing enormous work

In ayah 18 the Hereafter is not called the Hereafter. It is called **ghad**, "tomorrow" — the day after today. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws several things out of that choice.

**First, it shrinks this world.** If the coming life is "tomorrow," then this entire world, in relation to the Hereafter, is like a single day. And even that comparison is hard to hold in the mind, because the Hereafter is eternal and will exist without end, while the age of the human world is said to be a few thousand years, and reckoned from the creation of the heaven and the earth it would extend to a few million — in any case a limited period, which is no comparison to an unlimited one.
