Some traditions state: *the entire world is a day, and on that day we fast.* Anyway, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, neither figure is really the important one for a human individual: *every individual's world is made up of the days and years of his own age.* Every person should be able to realise how short a period that is next to the eternity of the Hereafter.

**Second, it settles the doubt.** The Day of Resurrection is as certain as the arrival of tomorrow after today, which is a stark reality no one doubts. The Hereafter, likewise, is beyond any reasonable doubt.

**Third, it brings the Day close.** Just as tomorrow is not far from today, the Day of Resurrection will happen very soon after this world. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Hour arrives in two phases. The first phase is personal: when an individual dies, his Hour is already established, as stated in a tradition — *he who dies, his Day of Judgment has been established* — because the signs of the next world start from the grave and examples of reward and punishment come forward there. The world of the grave, the world of *barzakh*, is like a waiting room in this world which accommodates all types of people, from first class to third class; the waiting room of the criminals is the prison house. A person should be able to determine his own position and status in that waiting room. And the timing of that first phase has been made a puzzling thing: not even the greatest philosopher or scientist can determine with any certainty the exact time of his death, and every coming moment is fraught with the danger that one may not live to see it. The second phase is when the entire world — the heaven, the earth and everything else — will perish; and though that might take place after hundreds of thousands of years, it is very close in relation to the eternity of the Hereafter. In short, by calling the Day *ghad*, the ayah makes us conscious that Doomsday is not far off; it is as close as tomorrow, and it is even possible that it comes before tomorrow.

**"What it has sent ahead."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the second point: since the arrival of that Day is certain and near, everyone is invited to think about what he has prepared for it. This shows that a person's original abode is the Hereafter and his residence in this world is that of a wayfarer, so it is necessary to send something from here for the eternal abode. And it is obvious that no material wealth or property can be taken along from this world. There is only one way of transferring wealth from one country to another: deposit it in the bank here, and obtain the currency of the other country there. In exactly the same way, wealth spent in the way of Allah and the sacred laws of Allah implemented are deposited in the Divinely celestial bank, where the currency of reward is recorded in the celestial account-book; and when a believer reaches the eternal abode it is handed over to him without claim or demand. Note too that the phrase *mā qaddamat li-ghad* carries the general sense of both good and bad deeds: whoever sends forth good deeds will obtain the currency of reward in the Hereafter, and whoever sends forth evil deeds will be indicted there.

Ibn Kathir gives the same command in one sharp sentence: **hold yourselves accountable before you are recompensed**, and contemplate what you have kept for yourselves of good deeds for the Day of your return and of being paraded before your Lord.

## The morning the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah

Ibn Kathir preserves the scene. Imam Ahmad recorded that al-Mundhir bin Jarir narrated from his father: they were in the company of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the early hours of the morning when some people came — barefooted, naked, wearing striped woollen clothes or cloaks, with their swords hung around their necks. Most of them, in fact all of them, belonged to the tribe of Muḍar. The colour of the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed when he saw them in poverty. He entered his house, came out, and commanded Bilāl to pronounce the adhān. Bilāl pronounced the adhān and the iqāmah, the Prophet ﷺ led the prayer, and then he addressed the people. He began by reciting *"O mankind! Have taqwā of your Lord, Who created you from a single person…"* (4:1), until the end of the ayah. Then he recited the ayah that is in Sūrat al-Ḥashr: **"and let every person look to what he has sent forth for tomorrow."**

Then he called for giving: a man donated his dīnār, his dirham, from his clothes, from his ṣāʿ of wheat, from his ṣāʿ of dates — until he said, *even if it was half a date.* Then a person among the Anṣār came with a moneybag which his hands could scarcely lift; in fact his hands could not lift it. Then the people followed continuously, until — says the narrator — I saw two heaps, of food and of clothes. And I saw the face of the Messenger ﷺ radiate with pleasure, like gold. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "He who sets a good example in Islam, there is a reward for him for this act of goodness and the reward of whoever acted according to it after him, without any deduction from their rewards. And whoever sets in Islam an evil example, there is upon him the burden of that evil and the burden of whoever acted upon it after him, without any deduction from their burden."

Muslim recorded this ḥadīth via the chain of Shuʿbah.

Notice what the Prophet ﷺ did with "look to what he has sent forth." He did not leave it as a mood. That same hour it became dinars and dirhams, a moneybag too heavy to lift, and two heaps of food and clothes. And the closing words widen the ayah: what you "send ahead" includes not only the deed itself but the example you set — and, the ḥadīth says plainly, that works in both directions.

## Why "have taqwā of Allah" twice

Ayah 18 opens with *ittaqū Allāh* and closes with *wa-ttaqū Allāh*. Ibn Kathir defines the term itself: taqwā of Allah pertains to obeying what He ordered and staying away from what He forbade — not a vague feeling, but a two-handed relationship with the command.

Why repeat it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers three readings and does not force a choice. It could be for emphasis. Or the first command is for man to fulfil the obligatory and imperative duties and the repetition is to abstain from sins — this second explanation is given by Maulānā Ashraf Thānawī. Or, third, the first command to fear Allah is to send forth good deeds for the Hereafter by acting upon the imperatives set by Allah, and the second is to ensure that what is being sent is not fake or counterfeit.

That third reading is worth sitting with. Counterfeit deeds, in relation to the Hereafter, would be deeds that seem to be genuinely righteous but lack sincerity of purpose and the good pleasure of Allah: what was done ostentatiously, or for an ulterior motive, or an ostensible action that seems like an act of worship but has no basis in religion, which amounts to innovation (*bidʿah*). So the second command to fear Allah implies that for the Hereafter it is not sufficient merely to accumulate ostensible actions; what is sent forward must be genuine, performed with sincerity according to the rules set in religion. Spurious actions will not be acceptable there.

And the ayah's last clause seals it: *"Indeed Allah is All-Aware of what you do."* Ibn Kathir comments that Allah asserts He knows all of your deeds and actions; nothing that pertains to you ever escapes His observation, nor is any matter of yours, whether major or minor, ever beyond His knowledge.

## Forgetting Allah, and losing yourself (ayah 19)

Ayah 19 gives the exact opposite of the self-audit: *"And be not like those who forgot Allah, and He caused them to forget themselves."*

Ibn Kathir reads it as a warning of a matching consequence: do not forget the remembrance of Allah, otherwise He will make you forget to perform the good deeds that benefit you on your return — **because the recompense is equated with the action.** He then places beside it: *"O you who believe! Let not your properties or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that, then they are the losers"* (63:9).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a short and unsettling note on *fa-ansāhum anfusahum*: **it was not Allah they lost track of, but themselves** — they became unaware of their own loss and gain.

Such people are named *al-fāsiqūn*, the rebellious — those, says Ibn Kathir, who rebel against obedience to Allah, and who will earn destruction on the Day of Resurrection and failure upon their return.

## Not equal, and never will be (ayah 20)

*"Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of the Paradise. It is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful."*

Ibn Kathir explains that these two categories of people are never the same with regard to the judgement of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and he gathers the parallel verses that make the same point as a rhetorical question:

- *"Or do those who earn evil deeds think that We shall hold them equal with those who believe and do righteous good deeds, in their present life and after their death? Worst is the judgement that they make."* (45:21)
- *"And not equal are the blind and those who see; nor are those who believe and do righteous good deeds and those who do evil. Little do you remember!"* (40:58)
- *"Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous good deeds as corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat those who have taqwā as the wicked?"* (38:28)

Therefore, Ibn Kathir concludes, Allah asserts that He will honour the righteous and humiliate the sinners. And notice how the ayah ends — not with a balanced statement of two outcomes, but with only one side named: *the dwellers of Paradise, they are the successful ones (al-fāʼizūn)*. Ibn Kathir defines that success soberly: they are those who will earn safety and deliverance from the torment of Allah the Exalted and Most Honoured.

## The mountain (ayah 21)

Then the register changes completely. *"Had We sent down this Qur'an on a mountain, you would surely have seen it humbling itself and rent asunder by the fear of Allah. Such are the parables which We put forward to mankind that they may reflect."*

Ibn Kathir reads it as Allah emphasising the greatness of the Qur'an and its high status, and its being worthy of making hearts humble and rent asunder upon hearing it, because of the true promises and sure threats that it contains. Then he turns the image on the reader. If this is the case with a mountain — hard and huge — that if it were made able to comprehend and understand this Qur'an it would feel humble and crumble from the fear of Allah, then what about you, O mankind? Why do your hearts not feel softness and humbleness from the fear of Allah, even though you understand Allah's command and comprehend His Book? This is why the ayah closes by saying these parables are put forward to mankind that they may reflect.

**The tree trunk that wept.** Ibn Kathir cites here a ḥadīth he describes as being of *mutawātir* grade (transmitted by so many chains that its occurrence is beyond doubt). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had someone make him a minbar; before that he used to stand next to a tree trunk in the masjid to deliver speeches. When the minbar was made and placed in the masjid, the Prophet ﷺ came to deliver a speech and passed the tree trunk on his way to the minbar — and the tree trunk started weeping, just like an infant, missing the remembrance of Allah and the revelation that used to be recited next to it. In one of the narrations for this ḥadīth, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said after relating it: *you, O mankind, are more worthy to miss the Messenger of Allah ﷺ than the tree trunk.* Ibn Kathir then returns to the same argument: if the solid mountains would feel humble and be rent asunder from the fear of Allah, had they heard Allah's speech and comprehended it, what about you, O mankind, who have heard the Qur'an and understood it?

He sets two further verses alongside it: *"And if there had been a Qur'an with which mountains could be moved, or the earth could be cloven asunder, or the dead could be made to speak…"* (13:31) — which, he notes, he has explained elsewhere to mean that if there were a Qur'an having those qualities, it would be this Qur'an; and *"And indeed, there are stones out of which rivers gush forth, and indeed, there are of them which split asunder so that water flows from them, and indeed, there are of them which fall down for fear of Allah"* (2:74).

**Is it a figure of speech, or literal?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports both positions. On the first, it is a parable Allah uses to illustrate that if the Qur'an were revealed upon such a strong, firm and unmovable mountain, and the mountain were endowed with intelligence like man's, it would have submitted to the greatness of the Qur'an — nay, it would have been crushed to pieces. But man is too selfish and proud; as a result he has lost his natural intelligence and remains unaffected by the powerful message of the Qur'an. On this reading it would appear to be a hypothetical example: *if* mountains had sense or intelligence. On the second view, cited from *Mazharī*, some scholars have stated that reason and revelation both bear testimony to the fact that everything in nature has sense, perception and intelligence, be it a mountain or a tree — so this is not a hypothetical example at all but a stark reality. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves it there with *and Allah knows best.* Either way the rebuke lands in the same place, as Ibn Kathir put it: the mountain would break, and you are the one who actually understands the words.

## Living it

- **Do the audit the ayah asks for.** Ibn Kathir's line is the whole practice: hold yourself accountable before you are recompensed, and contemplate what good deeds you have kept for yourself for the Day of your return.
- **Convert while the exchange is open.** No material wealth crosses over. The transfer happens, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, by wealth spent in the way of Allah and His sacred laws implemented — recorded in the celestial account-book and handed over on arrival without claim or demand.
- **Give something today, even half a date.** That is what the Prophet ﷺ called for the morning he recited this ayah — and whoever sets a good example has its reward and the reward of everyone who acts on it after him.
- **Check the coin, not just the count.** On one reading of the repeated command to fear Allah, the second is about sincerity: it is not enough to accumulate ostensible actions, because spurious ones will not be accepted there.
- **Guard remembrance, because it guards you.** Ibn Kathir sets 63:9 beside this ayah — do not let properties or children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. Forget His remembrance and, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, what you become unaware of is your own loss and gain.
- **Let the Book work on you.** It is worthy of making hearts humble and split open when they hear it; a mountain would crumble under it. Why, then, does the heart not soften?

passages.title: He is Allah: the beautiful names proclaimed
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat bring Sūrah al-Ḥashr to a close with a sustained proclamation of who Allah is — a cascade of His names and attributes, beginning three times over with **"He is Allah."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the movement plainly: having urged people to be concerned about the Hereafter and having asserted the greatness of the Qur'an, the sūrah is concluded with a few of Allah's attributes of perfection. Ibn Kathir heads this same stretch "Glorifying Allah the Exalted by mentioning His Names and Attributes." The last word of the sūrah is about Allah Himself.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

The ayah immediately before (ayah 21) reads: "Had We sent down this Qur'an on a mountain, you would surely have seen it humbling itself and rent asunder by the fear of Allah. Such are the parables which We put forward to mankind that they may reflect."

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is emphasising the greatness of the Qur'an — its high status, and its being worthy of making hearts humble and rent asunder upon hearing it, because of the true promises and sure threats that it contains. If this is the case with a mountain, hard and huge, which would feel humble and crumble from the fear of Allah were it made able to comprehend this Qur'an, then what about you, O mankind? Why do your hearts not feel softness and humbleness from the fear of Allah, even though you understand Allah's command and comprehend His Book?

Ibn Kathir supports this with a report he prefaces by saying there is "a Hadith of the Mutawatir grade" to this effect — that is, he is telling us how strongly the report is transmitted, not merely relating a story. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had someone make him a *minbar*, the raised place from which he would deliver his speeches; before that he used to stand next to a tree trunk in the masjid to deliver them. When the minbar was made and placed in the masjid and the Prophet ﷺ came to deliver a speech, passing the tree trunk and heading towards the minbar, the tree trunk started weeping, just like an infant. It missed hearing the remembrance of Allah and the revelation that were being recited next to it. In one of the narrations, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said after relating the hadith: "You — mankind — are more worthy to miss the Messenger of Allah ﷺ than the tree trunk!"

Ibn Kathir also brings alongside it: "And indeed, there are stones out of which rivers gush forth, and indeed, there are of them which split asunder so that water flows from them, and indeed, there are of them which fall down for fear of Allah" (2:74).

That is the emotional temperature into which these three ayat arrive.

## The refrain: "He is Allah"

Notice the architecture. Ayah 22 opens *Huwa Allāhu alladhī lā ilāha illā Huw* — "He is Allah, beside Whom *lā ilāha illā Huwa*." Ayah 23 opens with exactly the same words. Ayah 24 opens *Huwa Allāhu* and moves straight into the names of creating. Three waves, each beginning by naming Him, each adding a further cluster of attributes.

On that opening phrase Ibn Kathir writes that Allah states He alone is worthy of worship; there is no Lord or true deity for all that exists, except Him; and all that is being worshipped instead of Allah are false deities.

## Ayah 22: knowledge, then mercy

**"The All-Knower of the unseen and the seen."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses this simply: Allah knows all things, visible or invisible. Ibn Kathir expands it — He knows all that pertains to the creations that we see, and those we cannot see. Nothing in heaven or on earth ever escapes His knowledge, no matter how great or insignificant, big or small, including ants in darkness.

That last image is worth sitting with. Nothing is too hidden and nothing too small to be outside what He knows.

**"He is the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"** — ar-Raḥmān, ar-Raḥīm. Ibn Kathir notes that he explained these two names at the very beginning of his Tafsir, so he does not repeat it here; he affirms that Allah is the Owner of the wide encompassing mercy that entails all of His creation, and that He is ar-Raḥmān and ar-Raḥīm of this life and the Hereafter. He brings three ayat as witnesses: "And My mercy embraces all things" (7:156); "Your Lord has written (prescribed) mercy for Himself" (6:54); and "Say: 'In the bounty of Allah, and in His mercy — therein let them rejoice.' That is better than what they amass" (10:58).

The ayah names His knowledge first and then His mercy, and neither is given a boundary: nothing escapes the one, and the other embraces all things.

## Ayah 23: sovereignty, purity, and majesty

Ayah 23 gathers eight names. Ibn Kathir works through them one by one.

**Al-Malik — the King.** "The Owner and King of all things," who has full power over them without resistance or hindrance. Nothing pushes back.

**Al-Quddūs.** Here the early authorities differed in emphasis. Wahb ibn Munabbih said it means "The Pure." Mujāhid and Qatādah said it means "The Blessed." Ibn Jurayj said it means "He Whom the honourable angels glorify." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the first line: "the Most Pure from all defects" — the Being who is free from all kinds of defect, deficiency and imperfection which are not in conformity to His supreme status.

**As-Salām.** Ibn Kathir defines it as "free from any defects or shortcomings that lessen or decrease His perfect attributes and actions."

**Al-Mu'min.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the same word, applied to a human being, simply means "a believer"; but applied to Allah it means the One who provides peace and safety, as explained by Ibn ʿAbbās — He provides safety and perfect peace to those who believe in Allah and His Messengers. Ibn Kathir reports three readings: from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, who reported it from Ibn ʿAbbās, that it means He has granted safety to His servants by promising that He will never be unjust to them; Qatādah, that Allah affirms that His statements are true; and Ibn Zayd, that He attested to His faithful servants' having faith in Him.

**Al-Muhaymin.** According to Ibn ʿAbbās and others, Ibn Kathir reports, this means "The Witness for His servants' actions," that is, the Ever-Watcher over them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah, renders it "Guardian," and notes from the Arabic lexicon *Al-Qāmūs* that its root is *hamn*, meaning to look after or take care of or watch over (reported via Mazharī). Ibn Kathir lines it up with "And Allah is Witness over all things" (58:6), "and moreover Allah is Witness over what they used to do" (10:46), and "Is then He Who takes charge (guards) of every person and knows all that he has earned?" (13:33).

**Al-ʿAzīz.** "He is the Almighty, Dominant over all things," says Ibn Kathir; therefore His majesty is never violated, due to His might, greatness, irresistible power and pride. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the name simply "the Almighty."

**Al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir.** Ibn Kathir reads them together: "The Only One worthy of being the Compeller and Supreme." He cites a hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ Collection in which Allah said: *"Might is My Izar and pride is My Rida; if anyone disputes any one of them with Me, then I will punish him."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives **al-Jabbār** as "the One who is dominant," and then adds a second possibility: it could also be derived from *jabr*, meaning to join broken bones — from which comes *jabīrah*, the bandage or plaster used in binding broken bones. On that view, the attribute would mean that Allah is the Being who sets aright every broken and useless thing, restores all losses, rectifies situations and mends every breakage. Both senses are reported, and the reader is not asked to choose between them.

On **al-Mutakabbir** — "the Lord of Greatness" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a genuinely useful piece of theology. The name is derived from *takabbur*, and that from *kibriyā'*, meaning greatness, which is one of the peculiar characteristics of Allah. Every greatness is attributable only to Allah, who is not in need of anyone; whoever is in need cannot be great. Therefore, if this word is used for a person other than Allah it is a defect and a sin, because the claim of greatness by a person who is not actually great is false and tantamount to claiming to be a partner of Allah in one of His exclusive attributes. So the word, when attributed to Allah, is an attribute of perfection; in respect of others it is no more than a false claim.

**"Glory be to Allah! Above all that they associate as partners with Him."** Having named Him al-Malik, al-Quddūs, as-Salām, al-Mu'min, al-Muhaymin, al-ʿAzīz, al-Jabbār and al-Mutakabbir, the ayah ends by declaring Him high above all that they associate as partners with Him.

## Ayah 24: the names of making

**Al-Khāliq, al-Bāri', al-Muṣawwir.** Ibn Kathir distinguishes them: *al-Khāliq* refers to measuring and proportioning; *al-Bāri'* refers to inventing and bringing into existence what He has created and measured. Surely, none except Allah is able to measure, bring forth and create whatever He wills to come into existence. And *al-Muṣawwir* — if Allah wills something, He merely says to it "be" and it comes to existence in the form that He wills and the shape He chooses, as He says: "In whatever form He willed, He put you together" (82:8). Allah describes Himself as al-Muṣawwir, who brings into existence anything He wills in the shape and form He decides.

So the three names are not synonyms stacked for rhetoric. On Ibn Kathir's reading they trace a sequence: measuring and proportioning, bringing into existence, and giving form.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on *al-Muṣawwir* with real wonder. He gives shape to everything He creates, having given particular shapes to all creatures whereby they are distinguished from one another. Every species has a shape distinguishable from all other species; within one species there are differences in shape between males and females; and there are uncountable differences between the shapes of the individuals of even one sex. The excellence of shaping is of such a high degree that the shapes of countless men and women differ from one another in a way that no face is an absolute copy of some other face. Had it not been so, no one could be distinguished from the other. This excellence and perfection of creative power belongs to none but Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the parallel with al-Mutakabbir: just as *takabbur*, the show of greatness, is not permissible for anyone other than Allah — since *kibriyā'* is His exclusive attribute — likewise, on this view, no one besides Allah is permitted to do picture-making, because that too is the exclusive characteristic of Allah, and picture-making is an implied claim of being an associate with Allah in this attribute.

**"To Him belong the Best Names."** Ibn Kathir notes that he explained this phrase in the Tafsir of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, and cites what the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah the Exalted has ninety-nine Names, one hundred less one; whoever then preserves them, will enter Paradise. Allah is Witr (One) and He likes the Witr."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the scholarly context: the Holy Qur'an has not given the exact number of these Most Beautiful Names; authentic prophetic ahadith have counted them as ninety-nine, and Tirmidhī has collected all ninety-nine in one narration. Many scholars have written full books on the subject of *al-Asmā' al-Ḥusnā*.

Note how the phrase itself is rendered — "the Best Names" by Ibn Kathir, "the Most Beautiful Names" by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. The names are not presented merely as accurate labels; the description attached to them is one of goodness and beauty. And the hadith attaches a promise: whoever preserves them will enter Paradise.

**"All that is in the heavens and the earth glorify Him."** Ibn Kathir connects this to: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein, glorify Him and there is not a thing but glorifies His praise. But you understand not their glorification. Truly, He is Ever Forbearing, Oft-Forgiving" (17:44).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two levels of meaning. The first is self-evident: the wonderful, marvellous and amazing things Allah has created, and the awe-inspiring and staggering shapes He has fashioned, proclaim the praises of their Creator in unuttered language. The second is that the word *tasbīḥ* — declaring Allah's purity — may be used here in its real and literal sense, because according to the authentic view everything in this universe has some kind of sense that accords with its ability, and the foremost requirement of this sense is to recognise one's Creator and pay gratitude to Him. On that premise, it is not far-fetched to conceive that everything in nature really declares the purity of Allah in articulate language, though human ears might not be able to hear it — which is what "but you do not understand their extolling" (17:44) points to.

Read alongside ayah 21, this lands hard. A tree trunk wept. A mountain would have been rent asunder at this Qur'an. Everything in the heavens and the earth is already glorifying Allah. And Ibn Kathir's question is still standing: what about you, O mankind, who heard the Qur'an and understood it?

**"And He is al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥakīm."** Ibn Kathir closes: al-ʿAzīz, the Almighty — meaning His greatness is never humbled; al-Ḥakīm, the All-Wise — in His legislation and His decrees.

Then his own last line on the sūrah: "This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Al-Hashr. All praise is due to Allah."

## Living it

**Learn the names.** The hadith in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs ties *preserving* the ninety-nine names to entering Paradise. Whatever else preserving may involve, it begins with knowing them — and this passage sets out a cluster of them to know: that nothing in heaven or earth escapes His knowledge, down to ants in darkness (ayah 22); that His mercy embraces all things and He has written mercy for Himself (ayah 22); that greatness, *kibriyā'*, belongs to Him alone, so that a claim to it by anyone else is false (ayah 23); that He is, on one reported reading, the One who mends every breakage and restores every loss (ayah 23); and that the One who gave your face a shape no other face copies is the same One (ayah 24).

**A reported virtue of these very ayat.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records from Tirmidhī, on the authority of Sayyidnā Maʿqil ibn Yasār, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stated that Allah appoints seventy thousand angels who pray for divine mercy for anyone who recites three times *aʿūdhu billāhi as-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm min ash-shayṭān ar-rajīm* — seeking refuge with Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Shayṭān — followed by the last three verses of Sūrah al-Ḥashr, *Huwa Allāhu alladhī lā ilāha illā Huw*. If he dies the same day, he will attain the status of a martyr; and one who recites the same solemn words in the evening attains the same status. (Reported via Mazharī.)

**And the heart these ayat are aimed at.** If the mountain would have been rent asunder, and the trunk wept, and everything in the heavens and the earth is glorifying Him in a language human ears cannot hear — then Ibn Kathir's question is the one to sit with: why do our hearts not feel softness and humbleness from the fear of Allah, when we do understand His command and comprehend His Book? That is what these three ayat are for: not information about Allah, but a heart brought to attention before Him.
